title: Prevalence and Consequences of Guideline-Directed Indications for Aortic Valve Replacement in the EARLY TAVR Trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: The current American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association valvular heart disease guidelines were published before several recent trials that provide greater support for early intervention in patients with asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis (AS). OBJECTIVES: This study sought to investigate the prevalence and clinical impact of American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Class II recommendations for AVR in the EARLY TAVR trial. METHODS: The EARLY TAVR trial randomized patients with asymptomatic severe AS to transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) with a balloon-expandable valve or clinical surveillance (CS) with conversion to TAVR based on development of ACC/AHA Class I indications. Patients in the intention-to-treat cohort were stratified by presence of a Class II indication for AVR at randomization. The primary endpoint of the present analysis was the composite of all-cause death, stroke, or heart failure hospitalization. Interaction tests were performed to assess whether the treatment effect differed by level of guideline recommendation. Timing of conversion to AVR in the CS group according to the presence/absence of Class II indications was also assessed. RESULTS: Of the 901 patients randomized to TAVR (N = 445) and CS (N = 446), 636 (70.6%) patients had no guideline recommendation, and 265 (29.4%) had at least1 1 Class II recommendation for AVR at the time of randomization. At a median follow-up of 3.8 years, patients with a Class II indication for AVR experienced higher rates of the primary endpoint (Class II: 24.5% vs no recommendation: 14.5%; HR = 1.78; 95% CI: 1.30-2.44; P < 0.001) and were more likely to have acute valve syndrome at the time of conversion. Compared with CS, the relative benefit of early TAVR on the primary endpoint was similar regardless of the presence or absence of a Class II guideline recommendation (HR = 0.62; 95% CI: 0.37-1.02 vs 0.61; 95% CI: 0.40-0.92; Pinteraction = 0.96). CONCLUSIONS: Among patients in the EARLY TAVR trial, Class II indications for AVR were present in almost one-third of patients at baseline. The benefit of early TAVR was consistent regardless of the presence or absence of Class II indications. These findings support the strategy of early TAVR over CS in asymptomatic patients with severe AS, independent of guideline indications. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03042104; Unique Identifier: NCT03042104.

title: Transcatheter vs Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement for Isolated Native Aortic Regurgitation: National Propensity-Matched Analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is well established for aortic stenosis, while its application for isolated native aortic regurgitation (AR) was previously off label and technically challenging. Comparative data between TAVR and surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) are limited. OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study was to compare patient characteristics and outcomes of off-label TAVR vs SAVR among patients with isolated native AR. METHODS: Using the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Medicare Provider Analysis and Review database, patients ≥65 years of age who underwent TAVR or SAVR for isolated native AR (2017-2023) were identified. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed to evaluate short- and long-term outcomes. Fine-Gray models accounted for death as a competing risk, reported as subdistribution HRs (SHRs). RESULTS: Among 9,859 patients, 1,742 propensity score-matched pairs were included, with balanced baseline characteristics (mean age 75.8 years vs 75.7 years; female sex 517 of 1,742 [29.7%] vs 528 of 1,742 [30.3%]). In the matched cohort, TAVR was associated with shorter hospitalization (OR: 0.33; 95% CI: 0.28-0.39; P < 0.001) and lower in-hospital mortality (OR: 0.62; 95% CI: 0.39-1.00; P = 0.048) but higher 30-day pacemaker implantation (OR: 1.73; 95% CI: 1.33-2.25; P < 0.001). Through 5 years (median follow-up 2.58 years), TAVR was associated with increased repeat aortic valve replacement (SHR: 2.04; 95% CI: 1.13-3.66) but similar all-cause mortality (HR: 1.14; 95% CI: 0.98-1.31) and heart failure-related readmission (SHR: 1.09; 95% CI: 0.98-1.21) between treatment strategies. CONCLUSIONS: In this analysis, TAVR was associated with shorter hospitalization and comparable 5-year survival as SAVR, although pacemaker and long-term reinterventions rates were higher.

title: Prognostic Impact of Paravalvular Regurgitation in Patients With Severe Low-Flow, Low-Gradient Aortic Stenosis Undergoing TAVR
abstract: BACKGROUND: Paravalvular regurgitation (PVR) is a frequent complication after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) and may influence clinical outcomes in patients with high-gradient aortic stenosis. However, its prognostic relevance in patients with low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis (LFLG-AS) undergoing TAVR remains incompletely elucidated. OBJECTIVES: This study sought to evaluate the prognostic significance of PVR severity in patients with LFLG-AS undergoing TAVR with current-generation prostheses. METHODS: This multicenter registry-based cohort study included consecutive patients with LFLG-AS undergoing TAVR from January 2019 to December 2024 at 17 high-volume Italian centers. PVR severity was classified using a 5-class grading scheme and stratified as <2+ (none/trace or mild) or ≥2+ (mild-moderate or worse) based on separation of Kaplan-Meier curves for the primary outcome. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause death and heart failure hospitalization up to 2 years. Propensity score-weighted Cox regression was used to estimate the independent impact of PVR severity on clinical outcomes. RESULTS: A total of 1,358 patients were included. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed lower event-free survival among patients with ≥2+ PVR at discharge compared with those with <2+ PVR. After propensity score weighting, PVR ≥2+ was independently associated with a higher risk of the primary endpoint (adjusted HR: 3.77; 95% CI: 2.88-4.95), as well as higher risks of all-cause death, mainly cardiovascular, and heart failure hospitalization. These findings were consistent across both classical and paradoxical LFLG-AS phenotypes. CONCLUSIONS: In this large, real-world study of patients with LFLG-AS treated with current-generation TAVR devices, PVR ≥2+ was independently associated with worse clinical outcomes after discharge, regardless of LFLG-AS subtype.

title: Right Heart Dysfunction in Valvular Heart Disease: Epidemiology, Prognosis, and Management Considerations
abstract: Right ventricular (RV) dysfunction is an important determinant of clinical outcomes across a wide range of cardiovascular pathologies. As the prevalence of valvular heart disease (VHD) increases with the aging population, the intersection between RV function and VHD will become all the more relevant for proper risk assessment, treatment selection, and prognostication. Even though RV dysfunction may not always be attributed to VHD, we aim to give clinicians, researchers, and regulators a deep understanding of how patients with VHD should be evaluated for RV dysfunction and treated when RV dysfunction coexists with VHD. We begin with a discussion of the epidemiology and diagnostic evaluation of RV dysfunction in patients with a variety of VHD subgroups, including right-side (ie, associated with the tricuspid valve) and left-side (ie, associated with the mitral and aortic valves) VHD. Attention is also given in that section to contemporary methods and evolving techniques for identifying and phenotyping different forms of RV dysfunction in patients with VHD. No single imaging test practically or comprehensively captures all degrees and forms of RV dysfunction in patients with VHD; therefore, the discussion emphasizes integrating evidence from different imaging modalities and hemodynamic assessments. The second component of the review discusses how RV dysfunction affects therapeutic options, including medical, transcatheter, and surgical therapies for VHD. The focus of the discussion is on the interplay between RV dysfunction in patients with right-side VHD, namely tricuspid regurgitation (TR). Unlike left-side VHD, where RV dysfunction is a marker of overall disease severity but does not necessarily indicate futility or nonresponse to therapy, right-side VHD and TR-associated RV dysfunction identifies a subset of patients where intervention may precipitate even worse RV function. The nuances of these interactions between ventricular and valvular function are the emphasis of this section, and we aim to provide a framework for understanding RV function in the context of these different forms of VHD. Finally, the review concludes with an eye to the future, discussing the ways in which RV dysfunction can be identified and managed with the use of novel techniques. This discussion is increasingly relevant as RV dysfunction and VHD frequently coexist, and accurate identification is critical to matching the right treatment for the right patient.

title: Tricuspid inflow E-wave velocity for the assessment of severe or greater tricuspid regurgitation: derivation and external validation of threshold values
abstract: AIMS: Current guidelines include tricuspid inflow E-wave (>100 cm/s by pulsed-wave Doppler) as a semiquantitative criterion for diagnosing severe tricuspid regurgitation (TR), despite limited supporting evidence. We assessed its diagnostic performance for identifying severe or greater TR, deriving and externally validating practical thresholds. METHODS AND RESULTS: Tricuspid inflow E-wave velocity was measured by pulsed-wave Doppler in consecutive patients with at least mild TR between December 2024 and February 2026. Among 178 patients (77±13 years, 65% women), TR was mild in 44, moderate in 61, severe in 44, massive in 15, and torrential in 14. Mean tricuspid E-wave velocity was 56±16 cm/s and increased with TR severity: 47±8, 50±10, 62±16, 67±13, and 77±21 cm/s for mild, moderate, severe, massive, and torrential TR. Only three patients had E-wave velocity >100 cm/s (one with severe and two with torrential TR). Using multiparametric echocardiographic grading as the reference standard, the >100 cm/s threshold showed 5.5% sensitivity, 100% specificity, and kappa 0.25 for severe or greater TR. As a continuous variable, E-wave velocity discriminated severe or greater TR with an AUC of 0.81. A lower threshold of 52 cm/s yielded 81% sensitivity and 67% specificity, whereas 47 cm/s provided 90% sensitivity and 43% specificity. External validation resulted in 94% sensitivity and 47% specificity. CONCLUSION: The guideline-recommended threshold of >100 cm/s is highly insensitive for detecting severe or greater TR. Lower cut-offs, particularly 47 cm/s, may be useful for screening to trigger a comprehensive multiparametric assessment.

title: Standards Defining Echocardiography Core Laboratory (ECL) in Clinical Practice and Research
abstract: Echocardiography is extensively utilized in both clinical practice and research due to its accessibility. Echocardiography core laboratories (ECLs) adhering to societal guidelines offer superior readings and interpretations compared with the on-site assessments by reducing measurement variability and enhancing study precision. In the present work, we aim to define minimum standards for clinical echocardiography laboratories and research ECLs based on recommendations from the American Society of Echocardiography and the European Association of Cardiovascular Imaging, as well as on expert opinion and our experience in European countries. Accurate acquisition of high-quality images is crucial for ensuring reproducibility, repeatability and reliability of the echocardiographic measurements. In addition to the commonly used workstations, an academic ECL must also possess the necessary capacities and skilled personnel to conduct sophisticated research projects. Personnel should hold advanced certification in echocardiography, indicating postgraduate training and experience beyond the basic cardiovascular ultrasound education. They should be capable of designing, performing, and interpreting complex echocardiography studies. Reproducibility of the ECL should be validated using a small, randomly selected sample, preferably in the early analytic phase. ECL readings and interpretations are superior to site-reported measurements and serve as the gold standard in observational studies and clinical trials. To ensure internal validity, an academic ECL should continuously evaluate/report reproducibility, repeatability and reliability. ECL should be formally acknowledged and accredited by an international scientific imaging society.

title: Liver radiomics on routine cardiac CT identifies hepatic stress states that predict heart failure
abstract: AIMS: Heart failure (HF) prevention remains limited because early multisystem cardiometabolic dysfunction is not captured by conventional risk tools. We evaluated whether liver radiomic phenotypes derived opportunistically from coronary artery calcium computed tomography (CAC-CT) identify imaging-defined hepatic stress states associated with incident HF. METHODS AND RESULTS: We analysed 59 237 individuals undergoing CAC-CT (CLARIFY: 46 028; Houston Methodist: 13 209). Liver regions were segmented and radiomic features extracted to derive a Liver Radiomics Score (LRS). The model was trained in a CLARIFY derivation cohort (Dtr, n = 9205), validated in a hold-out cohort (Dts, n = 36 823), and externally evaluated in Houston Methodist (Dext, n = 13 209). The mean follow-up was 1411 days (SD 760.1) in the pooled Dtr and Dts cohorts (1144 HF events) and 470 days (SD 596) in Dext (212 HF events). Continuous LRS was associated with incident HF [Dts: hazard ratio (HR) 1.63, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.52-1.74; P < 0.001; Dext: HR 1.04, 95% CI 1.01-1.07; P = 0.004] and remained significant after multivariable adjustment in Dts. Increasing LRS quartiles showed progressively adverse hepatic, haemodynamic, and cardiometabolic profiles and higher HF risk. Among 17 806 Dts participants with PREVENT data, adding LRS modestly improved discrimination across CAC- and PREVENT-based models (P < 0.001) and improved reclassification metrics (7-year net reclassification improvement up to 0.25; including integrated discrimination improvement up to 0.015). High LRS identified elevated risk in low-risk groups: among participants with CAC=0, high LRS conferred ∼2.5-fold higher 5-year HF incidence, and ∼2.9-fold in PREVENT-low individuals. CONCLUSION: In this large multicentre cohort, liver radiomics from CAC-CT captured hepatic stress states linked to HF risk and modestly improved risk stratification beyond CAC and PREVENT scores.

title: Percutaneous Coronary Intervention in Dialysis Patients: Insights from a Nationwide Registry Analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Trans-radial intervention (TRI) has become the standard of care for percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). However, in patients on dialysis, trans-femoral intervention (TFI) remains predominant to preserve upper-limb vessels for arteriovenous fistula despite heightened hemorrhagic risk. This study aimed to compare TRI and TFI in dialysis patients undergoing PCI. METHODS: We used the National Cardiovascular Data Registry CathPCI Registry to compare patients on dialysis who underwent PCIs with TRI versus TFI from January 2018 to June 2025. An instrumental variable analysis with the institutional proportion of TRI use was performed to assess the risk of access-site bleeding and other peri-procedural outcomes. RESULTS: Among 137,702 dialysis patients who underwent PCI, 28.3% of patients underwent TRI (n=38,901), while 71.7% patients underwent TFI (n=98,801). TRI was associated with a lower risk of bleeding at the access site (adjusted risk difference [aRD]: -0.35%; 95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.56% to -0.15%). Overall bleeding (aRD: -1.38%; 95% CI: -1.89% to -0.87%), access-site hematoma (aRD: -0.86%; 95% CI: -1.13% to -0.60%), myocardial infarction (aRD: -0.21%; 95% CI: -0.39% to -0.03%), and mortality (aRD: -1.07%; 95% CI: -1.64% to -0.51%) were also less frequently observed in TRI. Conversely, TRI was associated with a higher risk of stroke (aRD: 0.23%; 95% CI: 0.001% to 0.45%), driven primarily by ischemic stroke. CONCLUSIONS: TRI was associated with a lower risk of bleeding events, but the effect size was modest. The higher observed stroke risk highlights a potential ischemic trade-off and warrants further study.

title: Safety and Efficacy of Topical Nitroglycerin for Radial Artery Dilation (The RADial Trial): A Randomized, Placebo-Controlled, Double-Blind Clinical Trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: Transradial coronary catheterization is associated with a reduced risk of bleeding and vascular complications. Prior studies have evaluated nitroglycerin to improve transradial access by vasodilating the radial artery, but the optimal route of administration for preprocedural arterial dilation remains unclear. METHODS: In the RADial Trial (Radial Artery Dilatation Trial) patients undergoing transradial coronary catheterization were randomized in a double-blind fashion to receive either a placebo or topical nitroglycerin ointment (nitropaste). The primary outcome was the mean change in radial artery dimensions, assessed using paired t tests. Categorical outcomes were analyzed using odds ratio (OR) with 95% CI. RESULTS: A total of 260 patients (130 placebo, 130 nitroglycerin) were enrolled. Nitropaste significantly increased the mean diameter (2.65±0.6 versus 2.48±0.6 mm), circumference (8.37±1.63 versus 7.77±1.66) and cross-sectional area (5.63±2.28 versus 4.94±2.0 mm) of the radial artery, whereas no significant difference was observed in the placebo arm. Nitropaste was associated with a significant reduction in the number of skin punctures and risk of vasospasm (OR 0.34 [95% CI, 0.13-0.91], P=0.04). There was no significant difference between nitropaste and placebo groups in the odds of hematoma (OR, 0.32 [95% CI, 0.03-3.1], P=0.61), crossover to femoral access (OR, 2.29 [95% CI, 0.9-5.8], P=0.12), need for ultrasound-guided access (OR, 0.39 [95% CI, 0.13-1.15], P=0.13), and hypotension or headache (OR, 1.5 [95% CI, 0.24-9.2], P=1.0). CONCLUSION: Preprocedural administration of nitropaste significantly increases radial artery size and reduces the risk of vasospasm without causing headache or hypotension. REGISTRATION: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05239013.

title: Impact of Coronary Sinus Reducer on the Extent of Ischemia in Functional Stress Tests
abstract: BACKGROUND: The coronary sinus reducer is an established therapy for patients with refractory angina due to obstructive coronary artery disease who are not candidates for further revascularization. Although symptomatic benefits are well documented, its effect on objective measures of ischemia remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the association between coronary sinus reducer implantation and inducible myocardial ischemia assessed by functional stress testing. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed a prospectively maintained registry of consecutive patients undergoing coronary sinus reducer implantation between 2011 and 2024. Baseline assessment included Canadian Cardiovascular Society angina class, 6-minute walk test, stress echocardiography, and dipyridamole single-photon emission computed tomography imaging, repeated at 6 months. Coprimary outcomes were changes in stress wall motion score index and in the proportion of patients with moderate or severe ischemia on single-photon emission computed tomography. Clinical nonresponders were defined as no improvement in Canadian Cardiovascular Society class at 12 months. RESULTS: Among 153 treated patients, 118 had complete imaging data. Median stress wall motion score index improved from 1.38 to 1.23 (P<0.001), and stress left ventricular ejection fraction increased from 55% to 60% (P=0.019). The proportion of patients with moderate or severe ischemia on single-photon emission computed tomography decreased from 52% to 24% (P<0.001). The summed difference score, available in 45 patients, did not change significantly. Clinically, 86% improved by ≥1 Canadian Cardiovascular Society class at 6 months. CONCLUSIONS: Coronary sinus reducer implantation was associated with reduced inducible ischemia on stress echocardiography and with clinical improvement. The proportion of patients with moderate or severe ischemia on single-photon emission computed tomography decreased following Reducer implantation.
